utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Have the accused brought in, please. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: As soon as the photographers have finished their work -- can everyone hear me well? Are the interpreters ready? Thank you, thank you for coming a little earlier. Mr. Prosecutor, the Defence, Mr. Nobilo, Mr. Hayman, can you hear me? General Blaskic, you can hear me? Very well, we can begin then. I hope my colleagues can hear me too. Mr. Kehoe, we have only one witness for this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. How long do you think his testimony will take? What is the summary, what is the connection with the indictment? Will you explain that to us in summary form, but with precision and with completeness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. President and your Honours. The first and only witness today is a gentleman by the name of Michael Buffini, B-U-F-F-I-N-I. Mr. Buffini is now a civilian. During the operative time frame, i.e. 1993, he was an officer in the Royal Marine Corps. He was carrying the rank of Major while he was operating in Central Bosnia and prior to that time, he carried the rank of Captain in the Royal Marines. Mr. Buffini was in the first instance assigned to the Combined British Forces headquarters in Split and he will testify that during the period of time that he was assigned to this location he saw HV troops, and this is Croatian army troops, moving into the Prozor area; he saw HV troops obviously engaged in fighting in the Prozor area, and in that area during this time frame the fighting was taking place between the Bosnian Muslim army and the HVO, of which the HV was assisting. He will likewise augment that testimony with conversations of an ex Royal Marine, who noted that he was training HV troops for assignment in Bosnia to assist the HVO. As you know, Mr. President and your Honours, this particular evidence goes to the international armed conflict issue which is pertinent to all the grave breach charges, so while it does not necessarily go to the factual information set forth, it does go to the international armed conflict issue which those counts run through the entire indictment. The next instance or instances that Mr. Buffini will discuss, he will discuss his work in the Busovaca Joint Commission, which commenced on approximately 6th March 1993, and concluded in the latter part of May 1993. He will discuss the parties, the representatives for each side that attended that meeting, specifically Franjo Nakic, Blaskic's second in command who represented the HVO, and Dzemal Merdan, who was the representative for the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He will talk about Blaskic's authority in Central Bosnia -- again, he will talk about this very briefly -- and how soldiers would not contravene Blaskic's orders, and that to get things done, Blaskic's orders had to be issued, most often in writing. After the peace agreement is signed, or the cease-fire agreement is signed on 21st April 1993, of which this Chamber has heard, Mr. Buffini and the Joint Commission begin to work on various complaints to ensure that the cease-fire holds. Those complaints involve allegations of trench digging by the HVO; those trench digging allegations focus on the use of civilians and prisoners of war doing those trench diggings. There were also allegations that the HVO was using these prisoners as human shields. Those allegations went to two individuals directly during those meetings, Blaskic's second in command, Franjo Nakic, and the brigade commander of the Vitez brigade, Mario Cerkez. Those complaints were made on numerous occasions by the BiH, but also by the representative of the International Red Cross, who Mr. Buffini will testify was visiting most of these prisons. He will discuss the failure to turn over prisoner lists and the HVO being reluctant, while as trench digging was going on, to turn over witness lists and how HVO local commanders refused to turn over those lists until it was cleared by Blaskic himself. Those particular allegations, Mr. President, go to a variety of allegations. If we can take them in sequence, turning first as part of the persecution count in count 1, the latter part of Mr. Buffini's testimony will go directly to paragraphs 6.4 and 6.5. Specifically in 6.5, Mr. President and your Honours, you will see that the allegations in that paragraph of the indictment focus on forcing Bosnian Muslim prisoners and civilians to dig trenches and also using them as human shields. More specifically, Mr. President and your Honours, we turn to paragraphs 15 through 20, which again recount specifically the use of Bosnian Muslims for the digging of trenches and for the use of those Bosnian Muslims as human shields. I am sorry, I said paragraphs 15 through 20, I apologise, I meant counts 15 through 20 and that should be page 12 in the indictment. In short, Mr. President and your Honours, that is the focus of Mr. Buffini's testimony as it pertains to the indictment and I anticipate, Mr. President, that this testimony will be quite short. We will not cover ground that we have covered before and I suspect that the examination-in-chief by the Prosecution will be done in maybe 30 to 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Kehoe, I thank you on behalf of my colleagues for this complete overview of this testimony that we are going to hear. Mr. Registrar, can you have Major Michael Buffini brought in, please. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can he hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please tell us your identity while still standing for the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am Michael Leslie Buffini.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please read the solemn declaration which is being handed to you by the usher. MAJOR MICHAEL BUFFINI (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Major Buffini, you have agreed to come and testify at the request of the Prosecution in a trial of the International Tribunal against General Blaskic, the accused, who is here present. Mr. Kehoe, who represents the Office of the Prosecution, has outlined in main lines your testimony, that you were stationed in Split, then the focal point of your testimony, all that you saw in the Joint Commission in Busovaca, and then the complaints and various allegations that were made following the cease-fire. Mr. Kehoe will put a certain number of opening questions to you, then you will make your testimony which will speak in support of the indictment. After that, of course, the Defence will have questions for you and the judges too at the end of your testimony. Mr. Kehoe, you have the floor. Examined by MR. KEHOE

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. Buffini.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we commence, if once again both you and I can be mindful of our discussions, given the fact that the people up in the booth have to interpret. If we just ask for a gap -- if we take a pause between question and answer, it will be helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buffini, can you tell us a little bit about yourself, what you are doing now and tell us a little bit about your military career up until the time of your retirement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the moment I am an investment advisor working in Brussels. I have been doing the job for just over two years now. Prior to that, I spent some time in the Royal Marines on two different occasions. I joined the Royal Marines in 1977 as a marine, but was commissioned as an officer while I was still under training. I spent a year as an officer under training, and then deployed to Malta for my first tour with the platoon. I then went to Cyprus with the United Nations and served six months there, before deploying to Northern Ireland with a commando unit, having done a mortar officers' course, so I was trained as a mortar officer, and took my job in Northern Ireland in South Armagh. After that, I spent some time recruiting for the Royal Navy and the Royal Marines and then spent a series of staff jobs, which was really behind a desk doing either training, serving in the Falkland Islands and up in the Commander in Chief Fleet of the Royal Navy's headquarters in Northwood, where I was responsible for security of Royal Marines on board ships who were responsible for security of nuclear weapons and the general safety of the ships. At that stage, I resigned from the Royal Marines and left, went to Hong Kong and set up as an investment advisor for two years out there. I was then asked to rejoin the Royal Marines at the level that I had left, so I retained my rank as Captain and I spent another four years in the Royal Marines. Within that four years when I rejoined in 1991, I was asked to go to join Commander British Forces out in Croatia and to deploy up into Bosnia as well, so I spent six months working in that location. I then spent some time after that in Ghana, training up security teams out there, and my final job before I was invalided from the Royal Marines was as a drafting officer for 3,500 troops of the Royal Marines, so I was responsible for their jobs, where they were going and their movement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buffini, so you resigned from the Royal Marine Corps because of a physical problem, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not resign, I had to leave because my knees were in such a condition that I could not fulfil all my duties as an active service officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buffini, if we can, can we begin to discuss your period of time when you were sent to the former Yugoslavia, and in your own words, can you just describe to the judges when you went to the former Yugoslavia, what you did there and I think as we discussed, it logically falls into two areas, the period of time when you were assigned to the Combined British Forces in Croatia, and then the period of time when you were assigned to the Busovaca Joint Commission. So again, Mr. Buffini, in your own words if you could describe your experiences down there to the judges at this point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I arrived in Split on 15th January, and my task at that stage was as a watch keeper for Commander British Forces based at Divulje barracks. I also had another task, which was my primary task, which was as the officer commanding of the UK liaison officers and there were nine teams of two people, each with a vehicle which was known as a RB-44, a Reynolds Borton 44 vehicle which was fitted out with an INMARSAT satellite telephone, with the ability to fax messages from laptop computers. We also had fairly comprehensive range of radio equipment on board as well. The idea was that the UK LOs, as they were referred to, were able to gather information from wherever the British forces were deployed and bringing it back to the Commander British Forces based in Split. So I was responsible for tasking those teams and ensuring they were doing their jobs correctly. For the first six or eight weeks, my main task was as the watch keeper, which involved an eight hour shift in the headquarters of Commander British Forces, monitoring the radio nets and telephone links with all the different agencies that they were in contact with. So we had a direct link to BritBat, who were based up in Vitez, direct links with the UNHCR, who were based at Metkovic and other locations and obviously direct linked with BHC, UNPROFOR's headquarters at Kiseljak. So my job was to note on a normal watch keeping pad all of the incidents that were happening over that shift of eight hours that I was there. So as something happened, I would note it down and then either take a responsive action or call other people in to take the necessary action that was required. During that time of watch keeping, I also had to deploy to visit my teams who were based at Metkovic, working with the UNHCR. They were also based up in Fojnica, with the tactical headquarters of Commander British Forces, and we also had teams in Tomislavgrad, who were working with. NCE, the National Command Element. The idea behind that was for me to familiarise myself with the duties of these people, what they were doing and ensuring they were doing something which was productive and not a waste of time. Over that first six weeks, I determined that they were quite a few jobs they were doing which were a waste of time and asked if I could redeploy my troops to better positions and to become more involved with gathering of information which was more relevant to them. So we changed the deployment from Fojnica up to Vitez, where the troops there were working with the British battalion. We also had a request while I was still watch keeping that two of the teams joined a working group which I understood to be the Busovaca Joint Commission in middle of February, and I sent two teams up there to work with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buffini, we are talking about the year 1993, are we not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So that was the deployment of my teams and in the main, while I was watch keeping, that was really what was happening. So I spent most of my time in Split on the watch keeping desk, but also some of the time travelling throughout Bosnia, visiting the locations in Vitez, in Gornji Vakuf when we were working through there and travelling up to Kiseljak to obviously discuss the deployment of the UK LOs throughout Central Bosnia. At the beginning of March, end of February, I was asked by Commander British Forces, Brigadier Cummings, if I would deploy full time up to the Busovaca Joint Commission to assist them with additional security and with communications elements that they were able to communicate on a much better range than they had at present, which was very limited. So from the beginning of March, I then moved up to Busovaca on a full time basis working with the Joint Commission, where I spent the next two or three months, apart from the two weeks I had as my leave, R&R, deployed in that area. The workings of the watch keeping, I will cover that first, I think, several incidents which I think come to mind while I was travelling up and down the triangle was the identification of troops, coaches and other forces that were moving up and down "route triangle" into Central Bosnia. The intelligence cell of Commander British Forces had asked us to gather information whenever we were on the ground, so I was specifically asked to identify on any given time troop movements of Croatian soldiers moving up into Central Bosnia. There were two occasions when I witnessed that, and another occasion when as a watch keeper I recorded an incident that related to Croatian troops moving in and out of Central Bosnia. The first incident was when I was watch keeping, and about 1.00 in the morning we got a report that a coach with Croatian soldiers on board had had an accident with a hand grenade in the coach and that one of the soldiers playing around with the hand grenade had let it off and had seriously wounded himself. The Royal Engineers based en route triangle were the nearest British troops to that and had relayed the information back to me as the watch keeper. I asked for more information, and was told that they were Croatian troops, and that they had asked for a "casevac", in other words a casualty evacuation, by helicopter, of the wounded people so they could be taken down to Split for treatment in the hospital. I refused permission for helicopters to be used for that purpose, because at that time the directive for the helicopters was purely the assistance of United Nations troops and not to any other warring factions. Other incidents which I noted were on driving up to Prozor, going through Prozor, on up to Gornji Vakuf and Vitez, was following a convoy of about six coaches which were quite obviously Croatian coaches, because we could identify their licence plates of the vehicles, and the soldiers within them were from the HV, and again that was noticeable from the badges that they were wearing. While we were following this convoy, we received quite a bit of verbal or signalled abuse from the soldiers within the coaches. We followed them for about two or three miles going into Prozor, where they turned off and we carried on up to Gornji Vakuf. I had to come back either the following day or two days later, and I noticed again the same six coaches, but this time they were loaded with what looked like very battle-weary troops, some wearing bandages, obviously those who had been injured and they were moving back out of Prozor heading towards "route triangle". Again we got quite a bit of signalled abuse as we passed by those coaches. Those were typical of the types of incidents we were asked to report back on to Commander British Forces. Other things were the identification of troops, where they were located, any training establishments, any helicopter flights, any aircraft flying which was breaking the no-fly restrictions. Again, several times we witnessed helicopters flying which were not United Nations helicopters and also a training camp which was being very actively used within Croatia, just south of the border. If I recall, it was just outside Sinj, and on one occasion certainly while we passed by there, a lot of coaches were inside the barracks with countless numbers of men inside the barracks obviously undergoing training. Several days later, while I was watch keeping, I had reports that a convoy of coaches were identified travelling up "route triangle", again with Croatian licence plates, and from reports coming in from the call signs that were reporting back to me as the watch keeper, they were Croatian soldiers on board those trucks, on the coaches. That took me up to the time of really when I deployed to Busovaca. Once I deployed up to Busovaca, I had a briefing from UNPROFOR headquarters as to exactly what my aims were, what we were trying to achieve and the reality behind the British troops that were involved within that organisation. I had complained a couple of weeks earlier to my arrival up in Busovaca that our vehicles, which were very soft skinned vehicles, they had no armour, no protection, were being shot at while they were accompanying the European Community Monitoring Mission, the ECMM, so I had refused for my troops to assist with the ECMM while they had no armoured protection. We eventually got agreement from UNPROFOR headquarters that they would provide some vehicles for us to move around in which were armoured, so therefore gave permission for the UK LOs to become involved again in the workings with the ECMM. The aim of the Joint Commission, at that stage, the early stage, was to try and negotiate cease-fires and the removal of all the checkpoints that were blocking the road between Vitez and Kiseljak, predominantly in the Busovaca-Kacuni area. We had an ECMM monitor, myself and then Franjo Nakic and General Merdan as the main members of the Busovaca Joint Commission. Our requirement was to bring people in who were the local commanders from the various villages and the various areas and the idea was that we would be able to liaise with them to ensure that the checkpoints were removed, that any complaints were addressed and dealt with and that the free movement of United Nations vehicles, UNHCR vehicles could take place throughout the whole of that area. So it started off on a very limited basis. It became very apparent that to ensure that the checkpoints were removed, we had to address wider issues. This was investigating reports of maltreatment of villages, reports of snipers operating in various areas, reports of villages being shot at and hassled by what were deemed as thugs or other sides, troops coming into those villages and behaving in a very threatening. So we had to start off by investigating those complaints from both sides and being fair and even with them to ensure that we could then move to the next point, which was the removal of checkpoints. So it was a gradual, slow process of investigating, agreeing on certain conditions before restrictions were lifted. Our time at Busovaca was fairly short, because we could not stay in the barracks that we had there in the hotel and in the house that we had rented, so we agreed to move up to Vitez and carry on our operations from Vitez, working in the same Busovaca-Kacuni area. It became very clear at that stage that the difficulties were not just confined to the Busovaca-Kiseljak road and that we then had to take into account complaints and negotiations throughout the whole of the Lasva Valley area, so we changed the emphasis from the Busovaca Joint Commission to the Joint Commission. Just going back to the personalities in that commission, it was very clear to me that the people who had the authority in that meeting was Dzemal Merdan from the Army of BiH. He had the authority and he also had the -- probably the support of his seniors in that when we had to make decisions, he made those decisions and instructed his troops on the ground when we were on the negotiations. Franjo Nakic did not really have the authority, and on several occasions in the early days to start off with, before any cease-fires or any negotiations or removal of checkpoints could be agreed upon, had to resort back to Colonel Blaskic for his authority and for his permission to do things. It became a little bit frustrating from our point of view that Merdan could make decisions but often they would be delayed because Nakic had to report back and get authority from his higher command. This again became prominent when we were at Vitez as the Joint Commission, when we were negotiating cease-fires, negotiating repairs of telephone lines and water pipes which were broken. Again it was clear that the authority was from Merdan and we could do things with him and he would instruct his local commanders that whatever negotiations and commitments were given, they would be carried out. Most of the time that was not the case for Franjo Nakic, who would have to report back. I went on R&R on about 4th April, so left the area. At the time, the Joint Commission had resolved a lot of difficulties, we had opened the route between Busovaca and Vitez, we had got most of the checkpoints off the road and incidents of shootings, snipings, ethnic cleansing had reduced not altogether but certainly considerably from the time we had started off at Busovaca, so we felt we were becoming reasonably successful, although it was quite time consuming in getting the agreements, the word around the places. It was clear to me before I left that the person who had the authority in the Lasva Valley area and command of the Muslim troops was Merdan. They respected him, they listened to him and they did what he actually instructed them to do. From the HVO side, the local commanders would not necessarily accept Nakic's orders, and on several occasions when we went into villages or when we were negotiating simple routine things with the local commanders, when Nakic had given the instructions as agreed in the Joint Commission, the local commanders would insist that Colonel Blaskic had to give those orders and that they wanted a written order signed by Colonel Blaskic himself before they would act upon the instructions of the Joint Commission. So again, it was clear that Colonel Blaskic had a very firm grip of the troops that were in that Lasva Valley area on the HVO side, and that Franjo Nakic did not have the same authority that Merdan had. But we had achieved quite a lot of our aims, so when I left on 4th April, the whole place had quietened down quite considerably. I returned back to Split on about 19th April, after my two weeks leave, and was very surprised to hear, although I had seen obviously television reports of the outbreak of violence within the Lasva Valley area, the difficulties that were being experienced, so I was sent back up to Vitez to continue my work with the Joint Commission, and arrived back, I believe, on either the night of the 20th or early morning of the 21st, because on that day, there was a high level meeting between General Petkovic and General Halilovic, with the Joint Commission, Ambassador Thebault and Commander BritBat within the ECMM house. That was the day that the cease-fire throughout the whole of Central Bosnia was announced and agreed upon and all the criteria for that cease-fire, in other words the removal from the front-line positions to given locations of both sides, and that was clearly stated; the exchange of all prisoners by a given date; the drawing up of lists of all the prisoners that were being held by each side and the exchange of those lists; and the fact that there would be a cease-fire from a given time where no more shooting was to happen in that area. I accompanied General Petkovic and Halilovic while they were visiting troops on both sides in Vitez and Stari Vitez as additional security, but as part of my role as the Joint Commission with the ECMM. So we visited troops in Stari Vitez, talked to them, visited troops in Vitez to inform them that there was a general cease-fire and that there should be no more fighting and that they were to obey the instructions of the two Generals. They were there in person and they were giving orders to their troops on the ground. So from the Commission's point of view, we felt very positive about that, that with somebody of those ranks giving those orders, that the cease-fire should take place. The reality was while we were speaking to troops on the ground, the soldiers, the individuals in Stari Vitez and Vitez, that none of them had any intention of wanting to stop fighting, but would obviously try and do so, but the hatred from both sides was so very apparent because of what had happened at Ahmici and certainly from the Muslims' point of view, where they felt that they had not got any answers, they had not got any idea, or nobody had come forward to own up as to what had happened. So it became very clear to us that while the two Generals had signed the agreement, there was going to be enormous difficulties in ensuring that the troops on the ground were going to agree to that. We felt quite confident, though, that because the commanders, the local commanders from both BiH and HVO had been present at those meetings, that they would have the authority and be able to distribute that information down to ensure that the cease-fire happened. From the Muslim point of view, they found it very difficult to accept the cease-fire, and to agree to what had been said, because they kept asking for information about who had perpetrated the massacre at Ahmici, who was responsible, and when were the ECMM/UN going to do something about it. That caused great difficulties in any negotiations, because it always came back to that point, as to what was happening. So in our meetings, we found that when we were trying to exchange lists of prisoners that neither side would hand over the lists. The Muslims had prepared those lists but the HVO side had not, and were very reluctant in doing so. They found it difficult to identify where they were, they found it difficult to find right locations, and so there was a delay there from providing any information. We also had Claire Podbielski come in on two occasions very soon after that meeting on 21st April to the Joint Commission, where Mario Cerkez, we had asked him to come in, because he was the commander of the HVO troops in Vitez itself, and on certainly two occasions, Miss Podbielski from the ICRC was very adamant that the HVO were breaking the rules of the Geneva Convention in that they were using troops as human shields -- prisoners, sorry, BiH prisoners as human shields and they were also using the BiH prisoners to dig trenches in their front-line positions. On one, two, possibly three occasions when she did come into the house, there would certainly be BiH and HVO commanders present and on two occasions, Mario Cerkez was there. When confronted with that information, Mario Cerkez was very flippant, denied it categorically and said that his troops would not dream of breaking the Geneva Convention, because they understood it. But it became clear that from our point of view, with the prisoners lists not being exchanged and the difficulties that they were having in providing those lists that there must have been something there to delay that and the reality we felt was that they were using these prisoners to dig the trenches and to provide front-line positions. When we asked Mario Cerkez, he denied it categorically, that any of the troops would be used for those purposes. We also asked Nakic, Franjo Nakic if he knew of any of the troops being used for that and again he denied that the HVO would be using prisoners of war for those purposes. I did not at any stage speak to Blaskic himself, but we asked for the message to be passed on to Colonel Blaskic to give us some answers as to whether prisoners were being used for that purpose, but again from Nakic and from Cerkez, we got a negative, that they were not being used for those purposes. We also investigated at this stage prisoners, locations of where prisoners were being held from both sides and trying to get into those locations. Several times we were prevented from going into the prison locations because orders had not been received from Colonel Blaskic to allow us to come into those locations to visit those prisoners, despite the fact that we had commanders from the local area accompanying us. So we spent quite a bit of time trying to negotiate the exchange of these lists of prisoners, but unfortunately, the Muslims, the BiH were very reluctant in providing the lists, and again kept coming back to the fact that nothing had had done, nobody had said anything, nobody had identified the perpetrators of the Ahmici massacre, and that caused a lot of resentment in the early days after my return on 21st April, within our meetings, because when we asked for Mario Cerkez and Franjo Nakic to provide answers as to who had committed this, who had done this atrocity in Ahmici, their response was that they did not know, it must have been thugs or renegade troops who were not under the HVO command, and on one instance, Mario Cerkez actually said that it was the BiH themselves who had committed the crime, really to curry favour with the United Nations ECMM, so in other words making the HVO look awful while themselves looking good. We, of course, did not believe that at all and felt that it was very much troops in that area who had committed that, but while we were in negotiations with the Joint Commission, we never got any answers from the HVO as to who had committed it, whether they had arrested it or whether they had followed up any significant investigation into who had carried it out. The early days after 21st April, when we were trying to negotiate the release of prisoners, the exchange of lists, meetings were very tense, very difficult. I noticed quite quickly that Franjo Nakic had become a little bit of a non-entity in our meetings. It was clear he did not have the authority to decide anything that the others had agreed, and it was only when Mario Cerkez came into the meetings that we felt we could deal with somebody who had a little bit of authority, but each time there was an agreement that had to be agreed upon, Merdan would give the agreement that his troops would do such and such but either Mario Cerkez or Franjo Nakic would insist they had to talk to Colonel Blaskic first or go back and see him and discuss terms or what they should be doing about that. Again, it was very clear that Colonel Blaskic had full control of all the local commanders and very much controlled those troops in Central Bosnia. Certainly in my opinion of dealing with these people on a day-to-day basis over almost a three month period, most of the commanders that I met from the HVO were fairly scared of Colonel Blaskic. They would not normally do anything in disagreement to the orders that he had given. The Joint Commission after 21st April had the agreement that there would be, because of the cease-fire and that it would be set in place, a joint headquarters of BiH and HVO troops which would be set up in Travnik, so my role started disappearing as the agreement was reached as to who would form the BiH element and the HVO element of this joint operational headquarters, which was to be based in Travnik. We still went out on some investigations, we still tried to negotiate some of the difficulties, because there was still quite a bit of shooting, still quite a bit of ethnic cleansing going on with burning of houses and a lot of complaints about civilians being beaten up, being victimised and being harassed, so we continued our work up until almost the end of May, when the joint operational headquarters deployed into Travnik. At that stage, I deployed my troops into other locations and I moved back to Split and spent quite a bit of time working in Croatia, in Prevlaka and also visiting my teams in Sarajevo who were deployed there. I think it was on about 12th July when I eventually left the area, because my role up in Bosnia and Croatia had come to an end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Major Buffini. You told us what the Prosecutor had summarised for us before. I think now there are some other points that must be clarified. Of course, you are not going to have the witness repeat himself, but you may ask other questions which you feel would supplement the ideas that Major Buffini has already expressed to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Mr. Buffini, just several questions based on your testimony, and I would like basically to follow the sequence that you testified to, if I may. You noted that when you were assigned to the combined British Forces headquarters, you had occasion to travel up "route triangle" towards the Prozor area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was in that Prozor area that you observed the coaches with the HV troops.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you also noted that a day or so later, you saw the same coaches and more HV troops that appeared to be wounded, was that accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true, yes. Some of them were wearing bandages, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we show those locations on the map, can you give the judges an idea of who was fighting in that area during this time frame?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was -- we concluded from the information we had gathered, and this was all of the British troops who were deployed in those areas, reporting back to the watch keeper and obviously to the intelligence cell, that around the Prozor area, and to the east of Prozor, it was the HVO and BiH which were in conflict, and that there was very intense fighting in the area east of Prozor, between, as I say, HVO and BiH troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I could, Mr. Buffini, and with the court's permission, if we could address ourselves to the map on the easel, and I believe, Mr. President, that is Exhibit 29K.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We do not have a microphone up there, Mr. President, so if I could ask the questions and then have Mr. Buffini move up to that area, up to the map. If I could ask you with the yellow pen that is to your left to mark on the map "route triangle", if you could.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Route triangle" came up around the lake area of this map and more or less finished at the end of the lake. That came close to Prozor, which is here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you also take with the yellow pen and put a line through the city of Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is Prozor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buffini, with the red pen that is on there, could you circle the general location that you saw these coaches with the HV troops in, and could you mark that with the number 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the first occasion, we followed them on that road going into Prozor where I have identified, so we were held up behind them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you mark that with the number 1 next to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this period of time, were there British battalion forces deployed in Gornji Vakuf just up the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you receiving information from Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were receiving daily Sit Reps from the troops based in Gornji Vakuf, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you take the yellow pen and just highlight the town of Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also noted that you observed troops with the same coaches but wounded troops on your way back through Prozor going out on "route triangle" a day or so later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you mark that location with the number 2 and a circle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was on the fairly large bend in the road just north of Prozor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw these troops, these HV troops, as a professional soldier, did you conclude they had been in combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Wearing of bandages, looking very tired, all carrying weapons, they looked as if they had been in the field for about two weeks, just as a rough guide, knowing the feeling myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also noted that there was an area east of Prozor where HVO and BiH troops were in combat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you circle that area with the green and mark that number 3, if you could?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Buffini. Please have a seat. Again, following up, Mr. Buffini, on some of the indications that you made concerning your identification of these troops as HV troops, how did you conclude that these were HV troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The trucks or the coaches themselves had Croatian licence plates. The soldiers themselves that we saw had insignia on which had HV only and not HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buffini, when you say, "Croatian licence plates", what was on this licence plate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The licence plate was -- it had the Croatian, I suppose symbol on it, or the shield on it, and it also had the numbers which identified that it was from a Croatian location, not specific, but it was totally different to anything that was seen in Central Bosnia which was not Croatian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You noted that you observed the patches about HV?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you had any conversations, Mr. Buffini, with ex members of the Royal Marines which supported your conclusions that there were HV troops in the Prozor area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I met an ex Royal Marines NCO, Gus Bryden, in Trogir, I think it was probably 5th or 6th February. He was in military uniform wearing a green beret, which was our own Royal Marines beret, so we hailed him and he came and spoke to us over a couple of beers for about an hour. We asked him what he was doing and he said he was a mercenary out here with his son and was working with the HV army. When we asked him specifics, he said that he had been training raw recruits, young 18 year olds to 55, who had all been conscripted into the Croatian army over a two week period to ensure that they could go to front-line positions. When we asked him where these front-lines positions were that the HV troops were working in, he said some were going to Zadar and some were going up to Prozor to help with the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you in fact observe a training camp facility on the Croatian Bosnian border?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I witnessed a training camp, most of the time which was empty as we drove past on a regular basis, which was just north of Sinj, I do not know how to pronounce that, but it is S-I-N-J, which was not in "route triangle", it was still in Trogir. On one occasion I witnessed large numbers of men in that camp, all in military uniform, and assumed they were all under training for deployment to the front-line positions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Buffini, did you have an opportunity to go back past that training facility shortly thereafter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when we noticed the first time I think we were either going up to Vitez or coming back from Vitez. I had to deploy again a week later, whichever way it was, and on that occasion there was nobody in there at all, the place was deserted. It was also during the time I was watch keeping and again we had had reports coming in, while I was on watch, that coachloads of troops were being monitored moving up "route triangle", so that was the assumption that they had come from that camp moving up to Prozor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it would be fair to say, Mr. Buffini, that you saw these troops training in this camp, you received information thereafter that troops were moving -- around the same time that troops were moving to Prozor and you returned past that camp and the troops were gone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you as a soldier conclude from that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conclusion to be drawn from that was that troops had been in training, very much along the lines that Gus Bryden, the mercenary, had informed us, that they had had their training time and were now deploying to their front-line positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, I am delaying to allow the interpreters to catch up. Mr. Buffini, you also noted that you observed helicopter flights breaking the no-fly restrictions. Where did you observe these helicopter flights breaking the no-fly restrictions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three occasions. One was to the south east of Zenica, which was obviously a BiH area. We saw some helicopters, I think two helicopters at that stage landing in some fields in broad daylight. Did not see that number of troops getting out but we certainly saw them landing and a couple of people getting in and out. The second occasion was flying into Vitez, but we did not see them landing or taking off anywhere else, but they were -- I think it was one helicopter that was seen going into the Vitez area, towards Vitez town itself. A couple of other occasions which I reported to COMBRITFOR was around the Sinj Knin area, which was on the Croatian border.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With regard to this helicopter flight into Vitez, were you aware of the HVO in Vitez having a helicopters, or the HVO having helicopters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. At no stage had we ever seen HVO helicopters in or around Vitez, apart from that one occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we may, if we can shift to your period of time with the Joint Commission, both with the Busovaca Joint Commission and also the Joint Commission as it was in Vitez. You noted that Franjo Nakic was the representative for the HVO, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know what Franjo Nakic's position was in the HVO vis-à-vis the accused, Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From what Franjo Nakic told us, he was the second in command of the HVO troops in that Central Bosnia area, so he was the appointed representative at the meeting of Colonel Blaskic and was his second in command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also noted, Mr. Buffini, that Mr. Nakic often told you that he had to check with Colonel Blaskic before he made these decisions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this true both before the conflict and after the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, where there were decisions that were made which were a little bit above the normal, telling a local commander that he had to, for example, take a single checkpoint off a road, most things over and above that, Nakic would have to go back to Colonel Blaskic or report back or ask for further details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you in fact ever take Franjo Nakic back to the Hotel Vitez so he could consult with Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not personally take him back, but certainly I instructed my UK LOs on numerous occasions when asked by Franjo Nakic to go back to the Hotel Vitez, because Nakic had to discuss what had been covered in the meetings with Colonel Blaskic, so several occasions we took him back to the Hotel Vitez, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You noted during your testimony that the local commanders were in fear of Blaskic and would operate with a written order of Blaskic while they would not necessarily follow the commands of Franjo Nakic. Was there ever an occasion of any consequence during this time period where you saw a commander, an HVO commander, directly refuse an order of General Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no time where any other commanders directly defied Colonel Blaskic's orders, no. The only time I witnessed where there was a little bit of revolt, I suppose, was in the beginning of June, when the convoy of hope or the convoy of peace was travelling through Bosnia. As it was passing through Vitez on its way up to Tuzla, a number of vehicles got taken out by the commander from Busovaca, and were taken to an area to be searched for weapons, because that commander was convinced that the Muslims were conveying weapons and arms and ammunition in this convoy up to the Muslim positions. We were asked, called in to negotiate the release of those trucks, and to deal with the local commander, so we took Merdan along and Nakic along and the Commission. The Busovaca commander was -- had obviously had quite a bit to drink, he was very angry, he was very upset that this convoy had been allowed to go through, where his feelings were that they should all be searched before going through, so he had taken action himself to check these weapons for any ammunition. After about two hours of negotiating and having had about six or eight trucks searched thoroughly, everything taken off them, them stripped down to quite some extent, no weapons, no ammunition, nothing had been found on those trucks apart from aid and food. When we started to get a little bit annoyed that the commander would not release the trucks, we asked him if he had the authority of Colonel Blaskic to take these trucks. He was a little bit reluctant about coming forward, but we then said we would have to go and see Colonel Blaskic to express in our strongest terms that this should not have happened and his commanders were not doing that. At that stage, the commander agreed that these trucks could then be released and could carry on their way, but he was rather reluctant about the whole thing. I think that was the only serious incident where I saw anybody who did not carry out Colonel Blaskic's orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me move ahead, Mr. Buffini. Now we are going to move to your testimony concerning events after the cease-fire agreement was signed on 21st April 1993. I want to direct your attention to the conversations where the International Red Cross representative, yourself and other ECMM representatives informed Mario Cerkez and Franjo Nakic that Bosnian prisoners were being taken to dig trenches and were being used as human shields. Was it clear, Mr. Buffini, to both Nakic and Cerkez that the use of Bosnian Muslims to dig trenches and as human shields was a violation of international humanitarian law? Was that clear to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very clear indeed. Claire Podbielski had got quite angry at one of the meetings and had said it three or four times that what the HVO were doing was contravening the Geneva Conventions by using prisoners in such a way as digging trenches and putting prisoners as human shields. It was repeated, as I say, two or three times to Mario Cerkez and Franjo Nakic and other HVO and BiH commanders at those meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Buffini, who was Claire Podbielski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Claire Podbielski was the Red Cross representative, the ICRC representative working in Central Bosnia at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn to the issue concerning the prisoner lists. According to your testimony, allegations concerning Bosnian Muslim prisoners digging trenches and being used as human shields by the HVO was coming at the same time when ECMM was requesting these prisoner lists, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you noted -- what was your conclusion -- let me withdraw that. You also noted that there was some reluctance of the HVO to produce these prisoner lists, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the HVO were very reluctant in producing any of the lists of prisoners or identifying prisons where prisoners were being held, whereas the BiH had come up with the lists, but had refused to give them over until, obviously, the HVO had produced their lists, so there was no exchange because the HVO were very reluctant about giving anything over.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to note, I think we are covering ground twice and at a certain point I may become concerned that I may not complete my cross-examination in time to let this witness go today and not have to return. For the convenience of the witness, the court and the Prosecutor, I make that observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President, the question that I am asking is going to the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I must adhere to the concerns expressed that we should speed up our work as much as possible. The judges have done all they can to that end. I remind Mr. Kehoe that he said that he would complete his examination-in-chief in 20 minutes, and up to the present, except once I did not notice any repetition, but I did not want to interrupt, up to now I think the questions were quite to the point. In any event, we will not be having a hearing this afternoon, I say that very clearly, but I think that both the Prosecution and the Defence are aware of our time limitations. I think that we should agree on those limitations, but if not, we would have to take some further steps, so please, Mr. Kehoe, go to the point and to the essential. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and I am almost completed with approximately three more questions and I will be done. Turning back, Mr. Buffini, concerning these prisoner lists that the HVO was not disclosing, did the local commanders tell you who had to authorise the disclosure of those prisoners lists before they could give them to you and to the BiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we asked the local commanders for those lists, several of them stated that they would only hand over the lists when they had received written instructions from Colonel Blaskic to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last subject matter: during this time frame, did you and Henk Morsink have a discussion with Mario Cerkez where you requested to see a location where you had heard that Muslim prisoners were digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were out with the ITN news team and we had some complaints from the commander of Stari Vitez, the Muslim BiH side, that they had witnessed BiH prisoners on the front-line positions being used as shields and for digging trenches. We approached Mario Cerkez and asked him where this was happening and he denied it, and we asked him for further information as to -- we asked him permission to go into some of the front-line locations to check this. We covered other points on that discussion which lasted for about an hour and by the time we had got to the front-line positions between Stari Vitez and Vitez, there were no prisoners to be seen, but there were some signs of fresh digging of trenches in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From those observations, what did you conclude, Mr. Buffini?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conclusion was very much that prisoners were being used for the digging of trenches and to provide protection for HV troops by using BiH prisoners as human shields.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecutor would offer into evidence Exhibit 29K and the Prosecutor has no further questions of Mr. Buffini at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I fully agree. Very well. We are going to have a 15 minute break, not more, and then we will continue with the cross-examination. (10.55 am) (A short break) (11.15 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will resume the hearing now. Please have the accused brought in. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, you are now going to conduct the cross-examination, and take whatever time you need.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I should conclude in about an hour. I do have several documents to show the witness and that is why it will take longer than I would have hoped but it does take some time to show seven or eight documents which we may need sight translations of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In the future, I can say this for the Prosecution now, but it will be for the Defence later on, when you state a time period, the Tribunal would like as much as possible to have that time respected. I know it is not always easy. It depends on the flexibility and availability of the judges to adopt themselves as well, but does not mean that one can just go on as long as one wants without respecting the time which has been set. Cross-examined by MR. HAYMAN

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please construe my comment as a request, Mr. President, I meant it as such. Good morning, Mr. Buffini.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke of the units that you were responsible for as having certain communications equipment in their vehicles, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, can you tell us whether during your service in Split and in Bosnia, whether those units ever intercepted any radio or telephone communications of Colonel Blaskic that might be of assistance to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I am going to object to radio intercepts. That certainly was not part of any direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Objection sustained. This was not part of the examination-in-chief. Move to another question please, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said that you deployed your units to assist the Busovaca Joint Commission with its communications capabilities, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the intention, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you joined them to assist in this regard, did they have limited communications capabilities, the Joint Commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Joint Commission only had very small handheld radios, which was interpersonal communication between themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they not able, using the equipment that they had, to communicate within, for example, the operative zone of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not have that facility, which was why we provided the INMARSAT satellite telephone for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are referring to the ECMM members -- you include the ECMM members of the Commission when you make that statement, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even though they had portable satellite telephone fax equipment, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were using our satellite telephone system which we supplied to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described several sightings of HV troops.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First the grenade incident you referred to. Can you help us fix that in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That must have been either the end of January or very early February, because I was still watch keeping at the time, and obviously left the watch keeping towards the end of February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told where this accident with the grenade happened? Where were these troops when the grenade blew up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The grenade actually blew up while the coaches were on the higher ground of "route triangle" in what was known as the wooded section of "route triangle", which was very much a Bosnia area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could just help us again, the higher ground of "route triangle", is that east, south, west of Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is south west of Prozor and it is not on that map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with that report, were you ever given any information suggesting that those troops had either been in the Lasva Valley or the Kiseljak valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described driving, going yourself to Prozor and following a coach of HV troops for two or three miles. Did that coach stop somewhere? Did you see it stop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The coaches stopped in Prozor where we overtook them and moved past them, having been stuck behind them for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thereafter, did you ever receive any information that those troops ever went to the Lasva Valley or the Kiseljak valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No information at all, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you described some troops leaving the Prozor area with bandages and they looked tired and so forth, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any information that those troops had been in the Lasva Valley or the Kiseljak valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no indication that they had been in conflict in those areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, your belief is that they were not, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my belief, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you help us put a date on those latter two encounters, the coach you followed for two or three miles and the coach with wounded, injured, tired soldiers that you saw; when were those events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those events were both in middle to end of February 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your tour, both in Split and in Bosnia, did you ever receive any information that HV troops had been in the Lasva Valley or the Kiseljak valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall any information coming to me or hearing any information to that effect, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were in the Lasva Valley and/or the Kiseljak valley for about eight weeks of time, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was nearer twelve weeks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that time, you never saw any indication of HV troops, is that right, in those locations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described seeing a helicopter in the area of Vitez, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the time frame of that sighting? Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The time frame was very much while the Commission was based in Vitez, so it must have been either late March, early April or the latter part of April, but I think it was before I went on leave, so I would assume the end of March/beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you dating that from memory or do you have any records that would assist you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is from memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any markings on the helicopter that you were able to observe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was too far to see any markings, but it was definitely of a Russian make.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether helicopters were used for Medevac by both the HVO army and the BiH Army when they were available for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was our understanding that helicopters were being used for that, but nothing had been agreed because there was a no-fly restriction and even for Casevac, helicopters had not been given approval to fly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described soldiers in a training camp. Was that training camp within Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said I think in your last event involving HV troops, you obtained a report that HV troops were moving in coaches up to "route triangle", is that right? This is a separate incident that we have not discussed yet in my examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you help us date that report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was before April 4th, so I would suggest that it would be in March some time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And again, you have no information suggesting that those troops went to the Lasva Valley or the Kiseljak valley, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were deployed to Busovaca to assist the Joint Commission. Who was the chairman of the Commission at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two separate incidents. Prior to my joining and deploying troops, Jeremy Fleming was the chairman of the Commission, but when I joined the Commission myself, Mats Torping had just taken over as chairman of the Commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend all of the meetings of the Commission during the time period that you were either in Busovaca when the Commission was based there, or in Vitez when the Commission was based there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was still in theatre, I attended probably 90 per cent of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of the Commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that based on the founding documents of the Commission or based on some other agreement reached between the parties, written or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a decision which was taken by UNPROFOR at a later stage after the founding of the Busovaca Joint Commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that when the Commission was founded, the membership was limited to an ECMM representative and then three representatives from the BH army and three representatives from the HVO army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When it was founded, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen those founding documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I probably saw them at the early stages of my initial meetings with the Commission when I had first deployed troops to assist them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If the usher could assist and show the witness a document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are you trying to impeach the credibility of the witness, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour, I think the witness may be able to assist us in clarifying the origins of the Joint Commission, who founded it, what was it founded for, who were the members. I apologise that this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: -- is in English only at the moment. We will have it translated. Have you been provided with the document, Mr. Buffini?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recognise it as something I am used to seeing, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise on the back the signature of Jeremy Fleming, chairman Joint Commission ECMM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen that signature on a couple of other documents before, so yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you recognise it as Mr. Fleming's?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I take it that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The context for the formation of the Commission, was it your understanding that this Commission was formed in response to the armed conflict that had occurred in and around Busovaca in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in response to the armed conflict, but it was the difficulty of free movement of vehicles, mainly UNHCR and UN vehicles throughout the area which was the overriding factor of trying to negotiate clear use of roads in those areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you would agree the historical context was the Commission was founded in response to the conflict in January in and around Busovaca which created various difficulties for humanitarian organisations, the UN and the like, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn that in fact the HVO had lost substantial ground during that conflict in January to the BH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was aware from military intelligence briefings in Split, when I first arrived and while I was watch keeping, that that was to some extent the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke of the respective roles of, I believe was it General Merdan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I referred to him as Dzemal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a General in the BH army at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We suspected it, but we had no confirmation that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was known to you as the deputy commander of III Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nakic, what was his military rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, we were advised that he was the deputy commander of the HVO forces in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever told that he was the Chief of Staff of the HVO forces in Central Bosnia, or was that ever your understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that was not my understanding, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there a difference between a deputy commander of a corps and a chief of staff, in the British army for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the British army, yes, a clear distinction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is a deputy commander in the chain of command, whereas a chief of staff is in an executive position, not in the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said by 4th April 1993, the Busovaca Joint Commission had accomplished a great deal, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We firmly believed we had done quite a bit, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any doubts that the members of the Joint Commission on both sides had been working in good faith to accomplish those ends?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most instances, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said on occasion, local commanders would not act without a written order from Colonel Blaskic, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What types of matters did that involve?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One incident was access into a village controlled by a local commander. Other incidents after 21st April included the exchange or the handing over of lists of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever get the impression or form the conclusion that when a local commander did not want to accommodate you or wanted to slow down the process, he found it convenient to say he would not act without a written order from Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question again?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever reach the conclusion or form the opinion that local HVO commanders, on occasion, if they did not want to accommodate your request, or they wanted to slow down the granting of your request, they sometimes asked to see a written order from Colonel Blaskic on the matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not think that was the case. They would not do things because they did not have that authority in place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described one occasion when you I think characterised a local commander as hesitating to follow a directive of Colonel Blaskic and that involved the convoy or joy or convoy of hope, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that incident around 10th June 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On recollection, something in early June, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You have given one characterisation of that event and I would like to read you a somewhat different characterisation of it, and ask you if in fact it is a description of the same event or if you think it is a description of a different event. It is a paragraph of perhaps 20 lines, your Honour. I think it should be placed on the ELMO so the interpreters can follow better and I have copied the page so that all can follow. Indeed for the record, and I will put on the record where this is from, Mr. President. This is page 3 from a witness statement of Alistair Duncan, taken in August and April 1993 by, among others, Mr. Kehoe. If the image could be enlarged and moved up. We will be looking at the bottom half of the page, beginning where there is a slash mark next to the word "when". I will read it to you, Mr. Buffini, and if you could keep my question in mind when I am reading it: "When the convoy of joy was finally moved on, it took the specific authority of Dario Kordic with the Croats in order to obtain release. Dario Kordic was thus the key to the release. I had previously taken Blaskic to the Vitez bypass where the convoy had been halted for the second time. This was at the T-junction at the easterly end of the Vitez bypass where you could turn right into Vitez town. Blaskic was wearing his military helmet and flak jacket. The soldiers refused to allow the convoy to move, even when I used the name of Colonel Blaskic as an authority. The soldiers said quite categorically that they wanted the order to come from Kordic. They had the appearance of normal HVO soldiers in standard mixtures of green combat and camouflaged fatigues. To my knowledge, this was the only occasion when the 'standard' HVO troops refused to obey an order from Colonel Blaskic. During this incident, it became clear to me that it was Kordic who was controlling the actions of the local police and the civilians who were both blocking the roads and looting the convoy. The convoy was only released when myself, the ECMM Ambassador and the COS of UNPROFOR, Brigadier Ver Hayes spoke directly to Kordic, Blaskic, HVO officers and civilian officials at a meeting in the disused timber factory in the Nova Bila area." Mr. Buffini, is it your view that this is a description of the same event involving the convoy of joy which you described, or is this a different event, a different convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The convoy is the same, but that was prior to the incident we were involved in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean? Do you mean the convoy was stopped at multiple points? I thought you said that you visited the convoy when it was stopped around the Busovaca-Vitez T-junction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that about 20 trucks had been taken from that convoy. The convoy had gone on, but 20 trucks had been taken from it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go to try and retrieve those 20 trucks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Into Busovaca itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that where the trucks were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Brigadier Duncan there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was his 2IC I believe, and one of the company commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever go to the scene of the stopped convoy at the T-junction of the Busovaca-Vitez road and see Colonel Blaskic there trying to free the convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One other question, there is a term used in this description I read "'standard' HVO troops". Did you ever make any distinction in your mind between, for example, an HVO brigade and the so-called special units within the HVO? Do you know what I am referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you are referring to the special unit who always wore black, then there was that distinction. I only saw those once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have said that in your opinion, commanders within the HVO uniformly followed the orders of Colonel Blaskic during your tenure, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any contact upon which you could base that opinion with commanders of the group known as the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am afraid, I do not know the Vitezovi. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
