utterances.text: There was a unit named Vitezovi, which either was or had descended from a unit of the HOS. Are you familiar with that unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am familiar with the term HOS, but not the unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have any contact with any commanders or soldiers in that unit that would permit you to form a specific opinion whether commanders in that unit obeyed or did not obey the orders of Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. As I say, I never met the unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the military police within the HVO? Did you have any contact with them that would permit you to form an opinion about the degree to which military police commanders within the HVO either followed or did not follow the orders of Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my knowledge, I was not aware that there was a distinct difference between military police and HVO troops operating in and around the Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about the unit known as the Jokers within the military police? Did you have any contact or gain any information about them that might enable you to form an opinion concerning whether they followed or did not follow, or indeed were even under the chain of command, clear chain of command of Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only thing I had heard about the Jokers were rumours that they existed. We never confirmed their presence at any times we were working in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever learn any information along the same lines about a unit commanded by an individual known as Zuti, Z-U-T-I, in the Nova Bila area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not recall anything on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I would like to turn your attention to 21st April 1993 meeting at the ECMM house in Vitez. Did you attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was present at the ECMM house and attended part of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that during at least the part that you attended, that the subject matter of the meeting was how to separate forces and establish a demilitarised zone, if you will, between the forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you also agree that during the portion of the meeting you attended, there was no discussion of any atrocities or alleged atrocities in Ahmici, nor any requests for inquiry or investigation on that subject?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not believe that subject was brought up at that stage, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you described the Generals Halilovic and Petkovic touring the area and instructing their soldiers to obey the cease-fire, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. They were informing them of the presence of the cease-fire, it had been agreed by both of them and that the troops should respect that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree with the following statement, and I am reading from your statement of 2nd and 3rd April 1997, page 7, in the middle: "During this tour of the area, I used the Joint Commission interpreter to ask both the BiH and HVO troops that I met as to what they thought of the Generals' plan. No one I spoke to believed that a cease-fire would last more than a couple of days. They insisted that such crimes had been committed against their own families that revenge had to be taken." Do you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that that was a sentiment you heard from both the BH army and the HVO side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have described the issue of the treatment of prisoners and the exchange of prisoner lists. Let me ask you first, did you ever meet with Colonel Blaskic and discuss this subject?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall meeting him directly or discussing it directly with him, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that orders given by Colonel Blaskic on this subject were obeyed by the HVO forces and the local commanders; that is on the subject of exchange and release of prisoners and exchange of prisoner lists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We never -- it was quite some weeks before we managed to exchange any lists or exchange any prisoners, so I am not quite sure what you mean by "obeying".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you or did others in the Commission perceive that there was a problem moving forward with the agreed upon exchange of prisoners, which I believe was part of the 21st April 1993 agreement, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did that agreement become stalled such that you made a request or someone else on the Commission made a request that the parties re-emphasise, re-order, put additional pressure on their forces to follow that term of 21st April 1993 agreement? When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in most of the meetings we had following that 21st April meeting, so each of the Joint Commission meetings that we had on subsequent days; when lists were not forthcoming, it was stressed to them that they had to comply with the orders made on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If the usher could assist, Mr. President, I have a document I would like to show the witness. I do not believe this is already in evidence, but it may be and I apologise if it is. I could not find it on the exhibit list as a Defence exhibit, a prior Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Will you please check the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If this could go on the ELMO, I think it would be of assistance to the interpreters, your Honour. I would like to call your attention, Mr. Buffini, to the document which has a date of April 18th , 1993. It states in pertinent part -- there is a reference to the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There is a little problem for the interpreters, who do not have the documents in front of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could it be enlarged, that is helpful. There are extra copies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is better now, is it not? It is better. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: There simply was not time, your Honour, to distribute all the copies during the break we had, but I do have extra copies if it is helpful. There is a title in the upper left-hand corner which is slightly cut off now, "the cease-fire between the HVO and ABiH units". Then it reads, and I am not going to read the entire document: "On the basis of orders given by the HVO head of staff" et cetera, dated April 18th: "I command", and I will read the first two points: "1. All the subordinate HVO units are to stop immediately all combat actions against the units of the ABiH. "2. Exchange the detained soldiers and the civilians at once." Mr. Buffini, was this order on 18th April, 1993, by Colonel Blaskic, was it obeyed by the HVO? Were detained soldiers and civilians exchanged at once at a point in time soon after 18th April 1993? Did it happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not think it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also described complaints about trench digging, correct? Prisoners being taken out to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a complaint we heard, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also describe the ICRC having problems getting into prisons and seeing detained persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it was mentioned to us by Miss Podbielski once that she had difficulty getting in, mainly because of the access to those places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are complaints I take it that arose after 21st April, 1993, when the agreement was made for a cease-fire and for the other terms you have described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was when I was back there and became aware of them, yes, because I returned on the 21st.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have another exhibit for the witness, Mr. President. It is two pages, the first page is in BSC and there is an English translation only. So the exhibit will consist of two pages. If the usher could assist and place the English translation on the ELMO, concentrating, with the assistance of the technical staff, on the body of the text, the six or seven points of the order, thank you. Mr. Buffini, I would like to call your attention to this document, which is dated 21st April, 1993, again references on the basis of the order of the chief of HVO main headquarters, is addressed to both HVO brigades and other entities, including the military police and the Vitezovi special task force, and which states, following the word "order": "1. ICRC shall be ensured free access to all civilians. "2. Civilian population caught up in combat shall be respected and protected. "3. Detained civilians and soldiers shall receive humane treatment and adequate protection. "4. The identity of all the imprisoned and detained shall be reported to the ICRC and its representatives shall be allowed to visit the individuals detained or imprisoned." Let me ask you, this order of April 21st with respect to reporting the identity of detained and imprisoned persons, was that order carried out in a timely manner, to your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From our workings on the ground, no, the order was not carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After 21st April, there were problems in securing the release and exchange of prisoners and indeed in securing lists of prisoners, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That problem existed on both sides of the conflict, correct? The BH army was reluctant to give lists and for whatever reasons, technical, logistic or otherwise, the HVO was not able to quickly produce lists of detained persons, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask in the meetings of the Busovaca Joint Commission, did you ask Mr. Nakic or one of the other HVO representatives, "please redouble your efforts to get this term of the April 21st 1993 order enforced?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was stressed just about every single meeting after that time that we wanted to ensure that the criteria put down in that cease-fire order were met. Up to that point, they had not been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you have stressed that point at some meeting between the 21st and 24th April 1993 at a meeting of the Busovaca Joint Commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It had changed from the Busovaca Joint Commission to the Joint Commission; yes, it was stressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If the usher could assist, I have a further document, Mr. President, which again consists of a BSC original and an English translation, I think they should together be one exhibit, whether A, B, what have you, and again if the text, the primary text of the exhibit could be placed on the ELMO for the assistance of the interpreters. Again, if the English text portion, the body of the text could be placed on the ELMO, Mr. Buffini, I would like to call your attention to the document, the English translation. It is dated 24th April, reference is: "Treatment of civilians and prisoners. Order to all commanders of units in Central Bosnia Operative Zone (brigades and independent units)." It says "based on the request" et cetera: "I hereby demand from all units and members of the HVO to: "1. Respect and protect the civilian population in wartime. Civilians by definition do not take part in conflicts and therefore cannot be a target of attack. "2. Treat captured soldiers and civilians humanely and ensure they are appropriately protected. "3. Report the identity of all the captured and detained to the ICRC and enable ICRC representatives to visit them according to ICRC standard conditions." With respect to point 3, Mr. Buffini, is this what you were asking Franjo Nakic between 21st and 24th April 1993, to obtain some further pressure from above to secure lists of prisoners and the exchange of those lists, as well as ICRC access to prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were asking for the HVO to come up with those lists, which up to that stage they had not done. I do not recall getting numbers of lists for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this issue persist between 24th April and 29th April, that is in your view and in the view of the Commission members, insufficient progress was being made in terms of securing and release and exchange of prisoners and indeed in securing lists of detained persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it continued to be very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If the usher could assist, Mr. President, I have one last document, again an exhibit of two pages, front and back, both pages, an order and a translation in English only at this time. If the body of the order, points 1 through 4 could be placed on the ELMO to assist the interpreting staff. This document is dated 29th April 1993, 19.40 hours, re the release of detained civilians: "In order to promptly carry out the joint order of the chief of HVO headquarters and chief of BH army main headquarters of 29th April, I hereby order: "1. Immediately draft lists of detained civilians (men, women, children) including the following information", which is then specified: "Responsible: immediate subordinate commanders. Deadline: 30th April 1993, 10.00 hours. "2. Release all civilians (men, women, children) arrested during the conflicts between the BH army and the HVO. Responsible: immediate subordinate commanders. Deadline: 30th April 1993, 12.00 hours." Then I will skip to point 4 for sake of speed: "4. All released civilians must be guaranteed full safety in the locations in your zones of responsibility and you shall be held responsible for the situation in your zone of responsibility." Signed Commander Tihomir Blaskic. Do you recall when detained civilians in the Vitez area were released? Were they released on or about 30th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Round about that time, but certainly into May when we started getting sufficient information to ensure that some releases were made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Returning for a moment to your comment that local commanders always or almost always followed Colonel Blaskic's orders, did you ever have contact with the HVO brigade commander in Kiseljak that would permit you to form an opinion regarding Colonel Blaskic's ability to control or inability to control the HVO brigade commander in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe I only met the commander of the Kiseljak area once on one meeting, so I could not --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you do not have an opinion on that specific point, I take it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not have such an opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see him and it was early days in my visit there, so I really could not say an opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you a few questions about "route triangle" and the Prozor area. Are you aware that in approximately January 1993, the road north from Prozor to Novi Travnik was cut to the HVO in the sense that it was taken over by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was cut in various areas and made travel through there incredibly difficult, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are aware that these coaches of HV troops you have described in and around Prozor, they would not have been capable, without encountering BH army forces, of driving north on the road from Prozor to Novi Travnik and entering the Lasva Valley at that time, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would not have had access through the Gornji Vakuf area, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They would not have had access to the Lasva Valley through that route, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the times you have identified these coaches as either being seen by you or reported as having been seen to you, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had a conversation with a mercenary, Gus Bryden. He said he had trained HV troops to go to Zadar, as well as Prozor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zadar is in Croatia, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the mercenary Mr. Bryden ever tell you that he had trained troops or had any knowledge that HV troops had ever gone to the Lasva Valley or the Kiseljak valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he only discussed operating around the Prozor area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described an incident where you and Mario Cerkez and an ITN news team went to the front and saw recent evidence of trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mario Cerkez did not accompany us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went with the news team?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss or raise the incident with Colonel Blaskic, that incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not personally, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that when you give us your opinion on whether orders were followed, that is orders of Colonel Blaskic, or not, you are basing your opinion on orders pertaining to the matters you were involved in, which principally were cease-fires, passage of convoys, clearance or repair of roads, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience, Mr. Buffini. Your Honour, I have no further questions, subject to a review of the exhibits and determining whether any of them should be admitted at this time. I think we can do that later so that we can move forward now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are we going to have these documents admitted? There was some doubt as to the order of Colonel Blaskic of 18th April. Mr. Registrar, have you had time to check, no? The Prosecution has no objection to the admission of these documents into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At this juncture, Mr. President, we do, based on a review of these documents. If these documents in any form came from the Office of the Prosecutor, they could have very well come from the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and we have no source as to where they came from, if they were given as Rule 68 material. I do not want to belabour the point on all of them, but I think a review of each document is in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let us put it under a number provisionally then. They will be admitted into evidence and the Registrar will give us the number. You have some re-examination, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I do. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, of course Re-examined by MR. KEHOE

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked questions by Defence counsel concerning the route going up to Central Bosnia through Gornji Vakuf being cut at various locations, is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was asked if they were cut, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were questioned concerning the capability of HV troops moving through to Central Bosnia on that route, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the town of Fojnica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are aware, are you not, that the Croatians were moving troops up through Fojnica and into Central Bosnia, to Kiseljak and the Vitez region, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had every -- lots of reports to suggest that that was the case, but no real sightings of anything pertaining to that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your conclusion on the information you had was that the reason they were clearing the area east of Prozor was to clear this road going up into Fojnica so they could move into the central or the Lasva Valley area and the Kiseljak area, is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was our conclusion and was the conclusion drawn by the British military cell in COMBRITFOR, that a route was being opened up between Prozor and Fojnica, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So any indication that troops could not move from Prozor to Central Bosnia via Fojnica would not be true, because they could move that way, could they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We believed they could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked some questions concerning these documents that counsel has put before you. Have you seen all these before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first one, and I do not know what -- the number on the order of 18th April. Do you see that one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That order was issued by General Blaskic, was it not, when war was still raging --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, I am not hearing the interpretation very well. I must say that it is not the first time the beginning of the interpretation is not quite audible enough. Maybe it is a purely technical matter, when one interpreter takes over from another. That is my impression, that is all. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That order on 18th April, according to your information, because you were not there, war was still raging, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact on 18th April, one might say that the HVO had reached their highest territorial gains, is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could well have been, but it was very pertinent for them to draw to a conclusion at that stage, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you say, it would have been very pertinent to conclude the hostilities once they had taken the ground that they wanted, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good military tactic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me counsel, if counsel are allowed to lead their own witnesses, I have no objection as long as that rule will be applied to the Defence as well as the Prosecution. Virtually every question has been an extraordinarily leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, I think it is not up to the judges to decide, I think that questions by hypothesis are leading and Mr. Hayman, you are the one who produced these documents, so it is quite normal for Mr. Kehoe to comment on them with the witness. Try not to introduce your personal opinions in the question, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I will not. Before we go to the rest of these documents that counsel discussed with you, let me just discuss, and I will ask you a question concerning the paragraph in your statement that was read to you by Defence counsel, and specifically the troops that -- I am reading the last sentence, the troops that you talked to: "They insisted that such crimes had been committed against their own families that revenge had to be taken." Do you recall that portion of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not true, Mr. Buffini -- withdraw that. At this particular point, was the issue involving Ahmici very much present during the time of these cease-fire negotiations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from the Muslim point of view, it was paramount to them that that was their biggest problem to all negotiations, was nothing was coming forward about Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not true, Mr. Buffini, that the HVO troops expressed reservations concerning the cease-fire because they thought the Muslims would want revenge because of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was that fear, but also there had been incidents where BiH soldiers had killed HVO troops and civilians in certain areas, I was informed by the HVO troops, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was factors on both sides, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right, but the overriding factor was Ahmici and obviously the BiH were very very aggrieved by that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn back to these orders that Defence counsel was asking you questions about. We are dealing with the series of orders that were placed on the ELMO, and from the line of questions that were asked by the Defence, the line of questions would want to indicate that Blaskic's orders were not being followed, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the line of questioning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said during the cross-examination that you were at 90 per cent of these meetings, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely right at that stage, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Nakic -- excuse me. Did Nakic or Cerkez ever indicate to you or to anybody else at this meeting that an HVO commander or a soldier was disciplined for failure to comply with the orders of Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, on no occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they ever bring any indication to you that someone was removed from their position, prosecuted, or in any fashion punished for a failure to comply with Blaskic's orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not that I can recall at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this period of time, you continued to receive information that the HVO had prisoners digging trenches and being used as human shields, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had complaints from the BiH that that was still happening, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Buffini, I think you testified in cross-examination that when you attempted to get into prisons, they had no order from Blaskic to allow to get into those prisons, is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what we were told.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. I give the floor to Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Major Buffini.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the light of your statements, you may be in a position to assist the Tribunal in clarifying some specific points. Among your statements, you mentioned in essence, I tried to write it, that Colonel Blaskic controlled all troops in Central Bosnia. Then you mentioned all commanders were scared from Blaskic and would not do anything in disagreement with his orders, and that Franjo Nakic had to go back to him to refer for any serious decision. In the light of this statement, my question is, and you are free not to answer it: could an action of the dimension of the events and the destructions of Stari Vitez and Ahmici take place without the order of this, what you called, controlling commander? Could it take place without his orders, or vice versa, could an order given by this commander to refrain from such actions be disregarded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first part of the question, could something like that have happened without the authority and the order of somebody like Colonel Blaskic take place: no. The scale of the operation and the extent of it was quite significant that there would have to be a large number of troops involved. That would have to come from orders of higher authority. The second part of the question was, could it have happened against the orders of somebody like Colonel Blaskic; again, my feeling would be that with my knowledge of the local commanders of the area, and their record for Colonel Blaskic, they would not have gone against those orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the same line, you mentioned that the Red Cross representative protested angrily with regard to the digging of trenches by prisoners in the front-lines, and the use of the prisoners as human shields. Was it within the jurisdiction of the commander at that moment, it was Colonel Blaskic, was it within his jurisdiction to react to this by stopping the use of human shields and stopping the digging of trenches, or was it beyond his jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It certainly was not beyond his jurisdiction, which is why we brought it up in the Commission meetings, so that the message very clearly got back through to him via Mario Cerkez and Franjo Nakic, for him to give the orders to cease doing so. It was also pointed out to the local commanders of those areas, where the incidents were happening, that this should not take place as well, so both the local commanders on the ground and also the message was asked to be directed directly to Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was up to him to stop it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the ultimate commander of the troops on the ground, so he should have insisted that his troops refrained and stopped immediately from doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Major Buffini. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I have a few questions to put to you; one which is very preliminary is this: the HV soldiers were Croatian soldiers from Croatia proper, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what we understood, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All your sightings of buses with HV soldiers were in Bosnia itself, Central Bosnia? How would you describe it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in Central Bosnia, because once you passed over the checkpoint south of Tomislavgrad, you were in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The buses which were taking the non-dishevelled HV soldiers were going away from the Croatian border or towards the Croatian border?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were going away from the Croatian border, north, further into Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the buses taking the dishevelled soldiers were going in which direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were pointing, they had not set off, but they were pointing in the direction to come back south from Prozor through back to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Back to Croatia. The inference which you drew from the condition in which you saw the dishevelled soldiers was that they had been engaged in combat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in a position to make any inference as to whether the place of combat was anywhere within Central Bosnia, or outside of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The inference was very much that they had come from the area around Prozor, which was in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. You have seen some documents put in evidence by learned Defence counsel. One is dated 21st April. Mr. Registrar, it would be convenient if I could refer to it by a number, but I do not know what number I should use. Will that be all right? You are not handicapped, you understand what I am referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are a military man and you are looking at a military document. Should I take it that your impression is that the document before you is in the standard form of a military document of that type?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It certainly would be along those lines, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The operative words here are these, the document is signed by Colonel Blaskic, and he says: "I hereby issue the following order." Would you say that those are words of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are as long as they are getting to the troops who are accepting the command, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at the top of that document, on the right-hand side, it seems to be addressed to: "HVO brigade commander 1-12; independent units in Central Bosnia Operative Zone; Vitezovi special task force." Would that signify that the officer issuing this document issued it on the basis that he had a right to exercise authority over the persons to whom the document was issued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge gained from your experience on the ground as to what this reference to independent units in Central Bosnia Operative Zone might have been intended to refer to? You see the reference there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but I am afraid I was not aware of independent units operating there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would see similar language in the companion document of 24th April 1993, the top right-hand corner has a reference to "independent units"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the operative words here are "I hereby demand". Those again would be understood by a military man to be words of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: British military commands would not "demand" anything, they would normally "order" something, but on similar lines, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. And the final document is dated 29th April, which uses like language with variations; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your conclusion would be, would it, that whatever happened in practice on the ground, the officer issuing using these documents considered that he himself had the authority to exercise control over the persons to whom these documents were issued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very much so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let us go to the Joint Commission. You spoke of Mr. Nakic, and you compared his disposition with that of Mr. Merdan; Mr. Merdan seemed to be able to decide matters on the spot, and Mr. Nakic tended to act ad referendum to Mr. Blaskic. Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was there any military matter on which Mr. Nakic took the position that this was an issue outside of the responsibility or authority or control or command of Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Outside the command of Colonel Blaskic? Was the question, "outside of Colonel Blaskic's command"? I am sorry, I did not quite understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me try to put it again. Was there any military matter in respect of which Mr. Nakic took the view that the matter was not part of the responsibility of Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not a military matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then Major, I would thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The presiding judge would like to thank you for answering all these questions that my colleagues have asked you. I have no further questions to ask you, the Tribunal is very appreciative of your having come here at the invitation of the Prosecutor for this long testimony. It now sends you back to your civilian activities and we can therefore ask the Registrar to have you accompanied outside the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This testimony completes the work that we are doing in December. We will resume in January and I think I can tell you the date that we will resume, but I have some hesitations because the schedule frequently changes. In fact it changes from hour to hour, but as things stand now we will resume on 19th January but at 2.00 for a long afternoon, that will be one of the new formulae. Perhaps I am wrong, but it seems to me that that is the schedule that was given this morning, that is from 1400 hours on 19th January, this will go until 7.00. This is a system we will use. This will not be used every week, but there will be certain times we will share the courtroom with another trial taking place in the morning, or sometimes we will reverse the order. In any case, this will be communicated to you in due fashion by the Registrar, but we have not completed all of the plans, so that we can at least say that we will begin at 2.00 on 19th January and continue until 7.00 in the evening, so that means that will give us a day almost equivalent to a full day. Therefore we now adjourn the hearing. (12.30 pm)
